title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Text Sequences
summary: This document describes the JSON text sequence format and the media type application/json-seq. A sequence is any number of JSON texts, encoded in UTF-8, each prefixed by an ASCII Record Separator character. This helps stream many JSON values one after another.

plainLanguage.summary: JSON is good at describing one value. Describing a long list of them means writing a single array, and a reader cannot use any of it until the whole array has arrived. This RFC defines a different shape for the same job: a run of JSON texts, each preceded by one control byte and each followed by a line feed. A reader finds the boundaries by looking for that one control byte, so it can handle each value as it arrives and can recover if one of them is damaged.

questions: how to stream multiple json texts
what is a json text sequence
why does json-seq use the record separator character
how to parse truncated json in a sequence
subtitle: A way to stream many JSON values one after another, with a marker byte that lets readers recover from damage.

tldr.problem: JSON is a convenient format for one value, but a large or endless sequence of values has to be written as a single array, which means the whole thing must be read before it can be used. The usual answer is a streaming parser, and those are not widely available, widely used or easy to use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a sequence format made of JSON texts, each preceded by a record separator byte, 0x1E, and each followed by a line feed, 0x0A. A reader can split the byte stream on the separator and parse each part on its own, and it can carry on after an element that will not parse.
tldr.outcome: A producer can write values one at a time and a consumer can read them one at a time, with no streaming parser and no end marker. The media type registered for it is application/json-seq.

facts.label: Sets of ABNF rules
facts.value: 2, one for parsers and one for encoders

today: RFC 7464 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the media type application/json-seq for the format it defines.

sections.title: Why a Sequence Format
sections.content:
The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) of RFC 7159 is a very handy serialization format. However, when serializing a large sequence of values as an array, or a possibly indeterminate-length or never-ending sequence of values, JSON becomes difficult to work with.

Consider a sequence of one million values, each possibly one kilobyte when encoded, which is roughly one gigabyte. It is often desirable to process such a dataset in an incremental manner, without having to read all of it before beginning to produce results. Traditionally, the way to do this with JSON is to use a streaming parser, but these are not widely available, widely used, or easy to use.

The RFC describes the concept and format of JSON text sequences, which are specifically not JSON texts themselves but are composed of possible JSON texts. JSON text sequences can be parsed and produced incrementally without needing a streaming parser or a streaming encoder.
sections.plainLanguage:
JSON describes one value at a time, and it is very good at that. The trouble starts when the values come in a series. The obvious encoding is one big array, and the reader has to receive the whole array before it can do anything with any of it. That is fine for a file on disk and useless for a feed that never ends.

There are streaming JSON parsers, but they are rare, little used and awkward. This RFC takes the opposite approach and changes the shape of the data instead, so that an ordinary parser can be used one value at a time.

sections.title: The Format on the Wire
sections.content:
Two different sets of ABNF rules are provided for the definition of JSON text sequences: one for parsers and one for encoders. Having two different sets of rules permits recovery by parsers from sequences where some of the elements are truncated for whatever reason. The syntax for parsers is specified in terms of octet strings that are then interpreted as JSON texts if possible. The syntax for encoders, on the other hand, assumes that sequence elements are not truncated.

JSON text sequences MUST use UTF-8 encoding; the other encodings of JSON, UTF-16 and UTF-32, MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage:
The format is described twice, with two different sets of rules, and the difference matters. The rules a reader follows allow for elements that have been cut short. The rules a writer follows do not, because a writer is assumed to produce whole values.

Everything is UTF-8. The other encodings that JSON allows are ruled out, because the marker bytes would not mean the same thing in each of them.

sections.title: Parsing a Sequence
sections.content:
In prose, a JSON text sequence as seen by a parser is a series of octet strings, each containing any octet other than a record separator, RS, which is 0x1E. All octet strings are preceded by an RS byte, and each octet string in the sequence is to be parsed as a JSON text in the UTF-8 encoding.

If parsing of such an octet string as a UTF-8-encoded JSON text fails, the parser SHOULD nonetheless continue parsing the remainder of the sequence. The parser can report such failures to applications, which might then choose to terminate parsing of a sequence. Multiple consecutive RS octets do not denote empty sequence elements between them and can be ignored.

The document does not define a mechanism for reliably identifying a text sequence by position, for example when sending individual elements of an array as unique text sequences. For applications where truncation is a possibility, this means that intended sequence elements can be truncated and can even be missing entirely, so a reference to an nth element would be unreliable. There is no end of sequence indicator.
sections.plainLanguage:
To read the format, a parser collects the bytes between one marker byte and the next, and tries to read them as a JSON value. The marker byte is 0x1E, called the record separator.

If the bytes between two markers are not a valid JSON value, the parser is told to carry on with the rest of the sequence and report the failure, rather than stopping. Two markers in a row are simply ignored.

Two things the format does not give you. There is no end marker, so the reader cannot tell the end of the stream from a pause. And there is no numbering, so if an element is truncated or missing, there is no way to tell which one it was.

sections.title: Producing a Sequence
sections.content:
In prose, a JSON text sequence as written by an encoder is any number of JSON texts, each encoded in UTF-8, each preceded by one ASCII RS character, and each followed by a line feed, LF. Since RS is an ASCII control character, it may only appear inside JSON strings in escaped form, and since RS may not appear in a JSON text in any other form, RS unambiguously delimits the start of any element in the sequence. RS is sufficient to unambiguously delimit all top-level JSON value types other than numbers. Following each JSON text with a line feed allows detection of truncated JSON texts consisting of a number at the top level.

JSON text sequence encoders are expected to ensure that the sequence elements are properly formed. When the encoder does the JSON text encoding itself, the sequence elements will naturally be properly formed. When it accepts already-encoded JSON texts, it ought to parse them before adding them to a sequence. The RFC notes that on some systems it is possible to input RS by typing ctrl-^, or ctrl-v ctrl-^, which is helpful when constructing a sequence by hand in a text editor.
sections.plainLanguage:
Writing the format is the mirror image. Each value is written as UTF-8, preceded by the marker byte 0x1E and followed by a line feed, 0x0A.

The marker byte cannot occur inside a JSON value except in escaped form inside a string, so finding one always means the start of the next value. The line feed is what makes a truncated number detectable, and that is covered in the next section.

A writer is expected to make sure each value is complete. If the writer is handed values that are already encoded, it should check them before adding them to the sequence.

sections.title: Malformed and Truncated Elements
sections.content:
JSON text sequence parsers should not abort when an octet string contains a malformed JSON text. Instead, the parser should skip to the next RS. Such a situation may arise in contexts where, for example, data appended to log files is truncated by the filesystem because of a crash or an administrative process termination.

Incremental JSON text parsers may be used, though of course a failure to parse a given text may result after first producing some incremental parse results. Sequence parsers should have an option to warn about truncated JSON texts.

While objects, arrays and strings are self-delimited in JSON texts, the numbers and the values true, false and null are not: only whitespace can delimit those four kinds of value. The sequence format therefore uses 0x0A as a canary octet to detect truncation. Parsers MUST check that any JSON texts that are a top-level number, or that might be true, false or null, include JSON whitespace, at least one byte matching the ws rule of RFC 7159, after that value; otherwise the JSON text may have been truncated. The line feed following each JSON text matches that rule.

Parsers MUST drop sequence elements consisting of non-self-delimited top-level values that may have been truncated, that is, values that are not delimited by whitespace. Parsers can report such texts as warnings, including optionally the parsed text or the original octet string.

The RFC gives examples. The bytes for RS, then 123, then RS, might have been intended to carry the top-level number 1234, but got truncated. The bytes for RS, then true, then RS, might have been intended to carry the invalid text trueish. The bytes for RS, then truefalse, then RS, are not two top-level values, true and false; they are simply not a valid JSON text.

Implementations may produce a value when parsing RS followed by a quoted string and RS, because their JSON text parser might be able to consume bytes incrementally; since the JSON text in this case is a self-delimiting top-level value, the parser can produce the result without consuming an additional byte. Such implementations ought to skip to the next RS byte, possibly reporting any intervening non-whitespace bytes.

Detection of truncation of non-self-delimited sequence elements is only possible when the sequence encoder produces or receives complete JSON texts. Implementations where the sequence encoder is not also in charge of encoding the individual JSON texts should ensure that those JSON texts are complete.
sections.plainLanguage:
The rule for damage is simple: when the bytes between two markers will not parse, skip them and carry on with the next element. This matters for logs, where a crash can leave the last entry half written.

Truncation needs more care, because most JSON values say where they end but four do not. A number, true, false and null can only be ended by whitespace, so a value that was cut in half can still look like the start of a valid one. The trailing line feed is what gives those four a definite end, and a parser must treat a number or a keyword with no whitespace after it as truncated and drop it.

The RFC is careful about one trap: the bytes for RS, true, RS could have been meant as trueish, cut short. And RS, truefalse, RS is not two values, it is one invalid value.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of JSON in RFC 7159 apply, and the format provides no cryptographic integrity protection of any kind. As usual, parsers must operate on input that is assumed to be untrusted, so they must fail gracefully in the face of malicious inputs.

Incremental JSON text parsers can produce partial results and later indicate failure to parse the remainder of a text. A sequence parser that uses an incremental JSON text parser might treat a sequence of RS, a quoted foo, a line feed, 456, a line feed, RS as a sequence of one element, while a sequence parser that uses a non-incremental JSON text parser might treat the same sequence as being empty. This effect, and texts that fail to parse and are ignored, can be used to smuggle data past sequence parsers that do not warn about JSON text failures.

Repeated parsing and re-encoding of a JSON text sequence can result in the addition or stripping of trailing line feed bytes from individual sequence element JSON texts, which can break signature validation. JSON has no canonical form for JSON texts, and therefore neither does the JSON text sequence format.
sections.plainLanguage:
The format adds no protection of its own, and it inherits everything that JSON already requires of a careful reader, in particular the rule that input is untrusted and must not be allowed to crash the parser.

Two traps are worth naming. A parser that reads values a piece at a time may report a value that a different parser would reject, and the difference between the two can be used to slip data past a parser that never complains. And a value that is read and written again may come back with a different number of trailing line feeds, which breaks any signature computed over the original bytes.

viz.caption: THE TWO SETS OF RULES, AS THE RFC PRINTS THEM

data.title: JSON text sequence ABNF
data.code:
input-JSON-sequence = *(1*RS possible-JSON)
RS = %x1E; "record separator" (RS), see RFC 20
possible-JSON = 1*(not-RS); attempt to parse as UTF-8-encoded JSON text
not-RS = %x00-1d / %x1f-ff; any octets other than RS

JSON-sequence = *(RS JSON-text LF)
LF = %x0A; "line feed" (LF), see RFC 20
JSON-text = <given by RFC 7159, using UTF-8 encoding>

viz.caption: WHAT EACH BYTE IN THE FORMAT DOES

items.title: Record separator, 0x1E
items.text: Marks the start of every element. It cannot occur unescaped inside a JSON value, so finding one always means a new element begins.

items.title: The JSON text
items.text: The value itself, encoded in UTF-8, with no IP or framing around it.

items.title: Line feed, 0x0A
items.text: Ends every element, and the whitespace it provides is what lets a reader detect a number or a keyword that was cut short.

items.title: No end marker
items.text: The format says nothing about where the sequence stops, and elements carry no position number.
